title: Grid operator says lights will stay on this winter after concerns
description: The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some o
body: The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine."While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them"."I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

schema.headline: Grid operator says lights will stay on this winter after concerns

title: Traitor behaviour splits opinion as paranoia deepens
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traito
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors.So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight.The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery. On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else?"To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet. "And I was."As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed.Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?"As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series.Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied. And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed."He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya. James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell." He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far. Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity. But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.Ahead of the round table, self-styled "Poundland Poirot" Sharon was living up to her nickname with a red herring theory about a perfume bottle being used to kill someone in plain sight. Ross's murder and the disorienting mission ultimately confused everyone, with the round table being the most random of the series so far. Leigh-Ann Pinnock, Bash Croft, Joanne and Jerry were among the accused, with Jerry - having survived murder overnight - banished for being "a professional pot stirrer. She's "planted more seeds than a farmer's market" – or at least that was Joanne's reasoning.Romesh's deadpan excuse was better: "I've long suspected she preferred Rob (his comedy partner and former contestant Rob Beckett) to me."Once again, the faithfuls were left to rue losing one of their own, with Jerry chastising them as she made her grand exit: "I told you so!"Leigh-Ann still had heat on her after Jerry's banishment, with her bright red - blood red? - leather-look long gloves drawing attention in the kitchen."I said they looked traitorous and villainous," she bemoaned.Back in the turret, as James A predicted, Maya and Kenny were not happy about his lack of action at the mission. "You hung us out to dry!" Maya chastised him.But he redeemed himself somewhat by declaring that he had finally got a taste for villainy."When I killed Ross Kemp in plain sight, I loved it!" James A told a delighted Maya and Kenny.It's only taken him three-quarters of the series to get there but better late than never.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

title: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
description: RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond, external to wildfires in Cyprus.In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spe
body: RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond, external to wildfires in Cyprus.In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend £45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground.It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added.Ministers are also pledging a £25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds."The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs.Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit."I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August."I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs."Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness, including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.

schema.headline: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says

title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
description: Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conferenc
body: Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully. Speaking at a press conference, he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials. The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation. BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.  Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October. Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

schema.headline: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network

title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming langua
body: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out."The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue"."But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented"."It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date."Hacking has been around for many years," he said."The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long."MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced."That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally."The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group."A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue."Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other"."Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

schema.headline: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found

title: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies
description: Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism,
body: Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime". Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed."It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time. "In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.The "Be Ready" campaign encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed". He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice. But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till".Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil". The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

schema.headline: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies

title: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok
description: Image source, Grandma DroniakImage caption, Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media ByYa
body: Image source, Grandma DroniakImage caption, Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media ByYasmin RufoBBC NewsNinety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties.The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that  allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks. With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month.The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren. From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life.'I'm showing it's not that bad to get old'"I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom.She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older."They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes."Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren.Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok."'I'm very picky about brand deals'On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff.She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits.Image source, Viv TruranImage caption, Viv Truran shares her colourful outfits with her more than 800,000 followersNow she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves."I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that."She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five.Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad".Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective.She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign."I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand."'I cry when people send me messages from around the world'Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium".Image source, Nonna GracieImage caption, Nonna Gracie has been dubbed "the internet's Italian grandma"Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades.Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job.Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off."I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says. Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table".'Virtual grandma' for followersBaker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world".Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says.Image source, Barbara CostelloImage caption, Barbara Costello says many people see her as the mother or grandmother they never had That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts.Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had"."Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy."Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on.She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children."It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life."

schema.headline: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok

title: Woman charged after police officer injured in Nottingham shooting
description: A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.Nottinghamshire Police said the officer was shot in the
body: A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.Nottinghamshire Police said the officer was shot in the foot after he approached a man and a woman at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.The male officer remains in hospital receiving treatment, the force added.Aisha Zaman, of Collison Street, Hyson Green, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.Police said the charge came after "consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service".Zaman has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham Magistrates' Court on Friday, police added.Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident, including two men, 24 and 30, and two women, 25 and 21, who have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both remain in police custody.Det Ch Supt Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said the "outpouring of support" for the officer had been "greatly appreciated". "We would just like to take this moment to thank the public", he added."We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation."He said officers were "still following a number of lines of inquiry", and anyone with information has been asked to contact the force.

schema.headline: Woman charged after police officer injured in Nottingham shooting

title: Harry Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in Rawalpindi run-fest
description: In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri
body: In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played.For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side.Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown.Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook – he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades.In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate.Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026.The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband.Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter – that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January.He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision.There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket.Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article"."I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said.In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer.As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos – he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers.As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level".The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament.Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022.Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport.To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan.In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won.Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what seemed an impregnable position, their bowling and fielding falling apart amid a growing realisation they were in danger of failing to defend a target of 430.There was some mitigation. Dew made the ball incredibly slippery, while their attack was weakened by the absence of the rested Jofra Archer and benched Adil Rashid.Nevertheless, the bowling was awful, particularly Sam Curran, who conceded 103 from nine overs to return the worst figures by an England bowler in an ODI. It was an error by Brook to continue to show faith in the left-armer, while not using the full allocation of 10 overs from either Josh Tongue or Gus Atkinson.It is one of the first major missteps of Brook's captaincy career and the sort of performance that shows England still have some way to go to be seen as serious World Cup contenders.Now, England will have to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final, to be played on 31 October, exactly 12 months on from Brook's horror show in Wellington.England need the sort of turnaround their captain has managed over the past year

schema.headline: Harry Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in Rawalpindi run-fest

title: O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?
description: Centre-back Liam Scales had by far the most touches of any Celtic player with 121, well ahead of left-back Kieran Tierney (79) and goalkeeper Sam John
body: Centre-back Liam Scales had by far the most touches of any Celtic player with 121, well ahead of left-back Kieran Tierney (79) and goalkeeper Sam Johnstone (69). Goalscorer Baur admitted they did not do enough to win and was at a loss when asked what needs to change. "How we played second half, last 30 minutes, we deserved it in the end," Baur said.When asked if he knew why his team collapsed in such a manner, he responded: "I cannot tell you, sorry."It can happen that you get a goal, they can score too, good team - you should then get control back, hold the ball a bit longer to take the momentum away from them. You should break that."Celtic did not get control back, did not break Celta's momentum and ultimately paid the price."I don't think Celtic are good enough, individually and collectively, to take on a team that's eighth in La Liga," former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner said on Sportsound."They moved the ball really well and Celtic couldn't get close to them."They are not good enough at this level. Celtic are paying big money for some players because the fans are demanding it and then they come in and aren't good enough."Their next European outing comes on 5 November as they host Besiktas, trying to reverse their continental woes. Whether they can or not is another matter.

schema.headline: O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?

title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
description: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood gl
body: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize."I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old."Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving.An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month.Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success."I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all."And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa."Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination.The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party.The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective.Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his £25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK.

schema.headline: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope

title: Tiger Shroff: Attack on Indian actor brings Bollywood's gangster past back into focus
description: On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans cong
body: On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor. Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad. "This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security. "There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

schema.headline: Tiger Shroff: Attack on Indian actor brings Bollywood's gangster past back into focus

title: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs
description: Image source, Hollie SharmanImage caption, Hollie Sharman spent hours searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolatedByEmily HoltHollie Sharman was
body: Image source, Hollie SharmanImage caption, Hollie Sharman spent hours searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolatedByEmily HoltHollie Sharman was convinced she was dying. She would go to hospital "four to five times a week" complaining of excruciating chest pain."I think the longest I spent in A&E was 13 hours," says the 25-year-old. But despite numerous tests, doctors could never find anything wrong.Sharman says she had "always worried" about her health as a child and remembers "making up any excuse" to get sent home from school and get into bed.Her 22nd birthday meal was spent in the restaurant toilets "having the worst panic attack I've ever had". That triggered years of health anxiety, with hours spent searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated. Constantly Googling symptoms "I was constantly Googling and using ChatGPT, every source I could get that could tell me what was wrong," she says. "I spent so long in the hospital. They'd tell me it's nothing, they'd check everything."I'd go home, but then my legs would feel weak, so I'd Google that and then it would say it's a sign of heart failure. So I'd go back, it was literally a constant cycle."At its worst, she "completely disconnected from everyone" and wouldn't reply to messages from family to avoid repetitive conversations.Sharman says her health anxiety also had an extreme affect on her relationship. "It got to the point that nothing he said would be the right thing."I would get upset because he didn't understand what was going on inside my own head. How can you tell someone everything's fine when I think I'm actually dying?"Image source, Dr Kirren SchnackImage caption, Dr Schnack says health anxiety is an "obsessional worry" about being seriously illClinical psychologist Dr Kirren Schnack says health anxiety is "a constant worry about being seriously ill or becoming seriously ill when you are not".Key signs can be "checking" behaviours, such as frequently examining your body, taking your temperature, blood pressure or researching symptoms online.Another is constantly asking the internet, friends or family for reassurance that you are safe and healthy, she tells Complex with Kimberley Wilson.Others may experience "avoidance" - not looking at their body or going to doctors appointments because they fear "the worst". Some may "take on the persona of somebody who has an illness", she adds."You may slow down your movements and stop exercising, you're treating yourself and your body and mind as if you are already ill." Image source, Hollie SharmanImage caption, Sharman says her parents understand her condition more after watching the videos she makes about health anxiety on TikTok Sharman was eventually diagnosed with health anxiety and health-related obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). She says her family and partner have been "incredibly supportive" and have helped her get to a "better place" with techniques to manage her anxiety."I'd write down my symptoms like 'chest pain, excruciating'. And then at the end of the day, I'd write that I was fine. "And then next time I'd have it, I'd have something to read and I'd be like, but I thought I was dying then and I wasn't."Sharman says her health anxiety "doesn't control her life any more"."You need to push yourself and do things when you're anxious, don't put your life on hold because I did for so many years."Complex with Kimberely Wilson How to deal with health anxiety. Listen now. How to manage health anxiety Dr Schnack says if you have a symptom that is "new, concerning or doesn't go away", it is "responsible health behaviour" to check the NHS website.If a symptom has not gone away within two weeks, she advises making a GP appointment. Here's when to call 111, 999 or go to A&E.And here are some tips from Dr Schnack that might help: Challenge worst-case thinking - give your brain other explanations for physical sensations; a stiff back might be poor posture rather than a serious illness.Limit reassurance-seeking - set rules and time limits on how often you ask friends or family about symptoms, and stick to them.Burn off anxious energy - take quick bursts of movement, like jumping jacks, to help process adrenaline and cortisol.Ground yourself - use strong sensory experiences such as holding an ice cube or tasting something sour or spicy.Breathing techniques - take a long breath through your nose, add a second inhale at the top and release it with a long sigh through your mouth.

schema.headline: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs

title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySima KotechaSenior UK correspondent at Southwark Crown Court   and Helen BushbyCulture reporterWarning - this report conta
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySima KotechaSenior UK correspondent at Southwark Crown Court   and Helen BushbyCulture reporterWarning - this report contains graphic contentThe friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after",  she said she "was just crying - really upset".The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually."He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her."He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.Russell Brand on TrialYou can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcastsShe said the woman replied "lots of times"."She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down".Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess"."She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her. "I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police. "She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go."She kind of put it behind her."Parents' statementsStatements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand. Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'."She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey."She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted."I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times."I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.Former boyfriend's statementThe woman's former boyfriend also gave evidence, telling the court she was "very upset" whenever she talked about her encounter with Brand, and that "she characterised it as an assault... she called it rape". Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC cross-examined the woman's former boyfriend and read parts of the statement he gave in June 2025, in which he said the woman had "come round" to having anal sex.When asked if he had said that, the witness replied: "Yes."The witness added the woman had "surrendered to the idea". "If I was being attacked, you either fight back or surrendered, it doesn't negate the attack," he added. Judge Mr Justice Bennathan sent the jury away until Monday morning, at the end of Thursday's evidence.He told the jurors that "we aim to finish the prosecution case on Monday", adding the defence case would not begin before Tuesday morning.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
